paragraphs: The Present and Probable Future Condition of the Three Races Which Inhabit the Territory of the United States

I have now completed the main task I set for myself. I have shown, as well as I could, the laws and the customs of American democracy. I could stop here, but the reader might feel that I have not met his expectations.

The absolute supremacy of democracy is not the only thing one finds in America; the inhabitants of the New World can be viewed from more than one angle. In the course of this work my subject has often led me to mention the Native Americans and Black Americans, but I have never been able to stop and show what place these two races hold within the democratic people I was describing. I have said in what spirit and under what laws the Anglo-American Union was formed, but I could only glance at the dangers that threaten that confederation, and it was equally impossible for me to give a detailed account of its chances of lasting, apart from its laws and customs. When I spoke of the united republican States, I made no guesses about whether republican forms would endure in the New World. And when I often referred to the commercial activity that prevails in the Union, I could not inquire into the future condition of the Americans as a commercial people.

These subjects are connected with my topic only indirectly, without being part of it. They are American without being democratic, and my main aim has been to portray democracy. I therefore had to put these questions off, and I now take them up as the fitting end of my work.

The territory now occupied or claimed by the American Union stretches from the shores of the Atlantic to those of the Pacific Ocean. To the east and west, its limits are those of the continent itself. To the south it reaches nearly to the tropics, and to the north it extends into the icy regions. The human beings scattered over this space do not form, as in Europe, so many branches of the same stock. At first glance one can pick out three races among them, naturally distinct and, I might almost say, hostile to one another. Education and law, as well as origin and outward appearance, had raised almost insurmountable barriers between them. But fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not blend, and each race fulfills its destiny apart.

Among these widely different families of men, the first to attract attention, superior in intelligence, power, and enjoyment, is the white or European, the preeminent man. Below him, in lower ranks, come the Black American and the Native American. These two unfortunate races have nothing in common: not birth, not features, not language, not habits. Their only likeness lies in their misfortunes. Both hold an inferior rank in the country they inhabit; both suffer under tyranny; and if their wrongs are not the same, they come, at any rate, from the same authors.

If we reasoned from what goes on in the world, we might almost say that the European is to the other races of mankind what man is to the lower animals. He makes them serve his purposes, and when he cannot subdue them, he destroys them. Oppression has, at one stroke, stripped the descendants of Africans of almost all the privileges of humanity. The Black American in the United States has lost all memory of his country. The language his forefathers spoke is never heard around him. He gave up their religion and forgot their customs when he ceased to belong to Africa, without gaining any claim to European privileges. So he remains halfway between the two communities, sold by one and rejected by the other, finding no spot in the universe to call his country, except the faint image of a home that his master’s roof provides.

The Black American has no family; woman is merely the temporary companion of his pleasures, and his children are his equals from the moment they are born. Should I call it a proof of God’s mercy or a visitation of his wrath, that in certain conditions man seems insensible to his extreme wretchedness, and almost develops a perverse fondness for the cause of his misfortunes? The Black American, plunged in this abyss of evils, scarcely feels his own calamitous situation. Violence made him a slave, and the habit of servitude gives him a slave’s thoughts and desires. He admires his tyrants more than he hates them, and finds his joy and pride in servile imitation of those who oppress him. His understanding has been degraded to the level of his soul.

The Black American enters slavery the moment he is born. Indeed, he may have been bought in the womb and begun his slavery before he began his existence. With no wants and no enjoyments, and useless to himself, he learns with his first ideas of existence that he is another man’s property, that this man has an interest in keeping him alive, and that the care of his life does not fall to himself. Even the power of thought appears to him a useless gift of Providence, and he quietly enjoys the privileges of his degradation. If he becomes free, he often finds independence a heavier burden than slavery. For he has learned in the course of his life to submit to everything except reason, and he knows too little of her dictates to obey them. A thousand new desires beset him, and he lacks the knowledge and energy to resist them. These are masters that must be fought, and he has learned only to submit and obey. In short, he sinks to such a depth of wretchedness that while servitude brutalizes him, liberty destroys him.

Oppression has been no less fatal to the Native Americans than to Black Americans, but its effects are different. Before white men arrived in the New World, the inhabitants of North America lived quietly in their woods, going through the changes of fortune, and practicing the virtues and vices, common to savage nations. The Europeans scattered the tribes, drove them into the wilderness, and condemned them to a wandering life full of inexpressible sufferings.

Savage nations are governed only by opinion and custom. The Native Americans lost their sense of attachment to their country; their families were dispersed, their traditions obscured, and the chain of their memories broken. All their habits were changed, and their wants grew beyond measure. European tyranny made them more disorderly and less civilized than they had been before. The moral and physical condition of the tribes kept getting worse, and they became more barbarous as they became more wretched. Nevertheless, the Europeans have not been able to transform the character of the Native Americans. They have had the power to destroy them, but they have never been able to make them submit to the rules of civilized society.

The lot of the Black American lies at the extreme limit of servitude, while that of the Native American lies at the farthest edge of liberty. Slavery does not produce more fatal effects on the first than independence does on the second. The Black slave has lost all property in his own person, and he cannot dispose of his own existence without committing a kind of fraud. But the savage is his own master as soon as he is able to act. He scarcely knows parental authority; he has never bent his will to that of any other person, nor learned the difference between voluntary obedience and shameful subjection; and the very name of law is unknown to him. To be free, for him, means to escape every shackle of society. He delights in this barbarous independence and would rather die than give up the least part of it, so civilization has little power over him.

The Black American makes a thousand fruitless efforts to work his way in among men who reject him. He conforms to the tastes of his oppressors, adopts their opinions, and hopes by imitating them to become part of their community. He has been told from infancy that his race is naturally inferior to the whites, and he accepts the claim and is ashamed of his own nature. In each of his features he finds a trace of slavery, and if it were in his power, he would gladly rid himself of everything that makes him what he is.

The Native American, on the contrary, has an imagination swollen with the supposed nobility of his origin, and he lives and dies amid these dreams of pride. Far from wanting to conform his habits to ours, he loves his savage life as the distinguishing mark of his race, and he rejects every step toward civilization, perhaps less from hatred of it than from dread of resembling the Europeans. *a He has nothing to set against our perfection in the arts but the resources of the wilderness, and nothing to set against our tactics but undisciplined courage. Our carefully worked-out plans are met only by the spontaneous instincts of savage life. Who can wonder if he fails in this unequal contest?

a [ The native of North America holds on to his opinions and even the most insignificant of his habits with a tenacity that has no parallel in history. For more than two hundred years the wandering tribes of North America have been in daily contact with the whites, and they have never taken from them either a custom or an idea. Yet the Europeans have had a powerful influence over the savages: they have made them more licentious, but not more European. In the summer of 1831 I happened to be beyond Lake Michigan, at a place called Green Bay, which serves as the farthest frontier between the United States and the Native Americans on the northwestern side. There I met an American officer, Major H., who talked to me at length about the inflexibility of the Native American character and then related the following fact: “I formerly knew a young Indian,” he said, “who had been educated at a college in New England, where he had greatly distinguished himself, and had acquired the external appearance of a member of civilized society. When the war broke out between ourselves and the English in 1810, I saw this young man again; he was serving in our army, at the head of the warriors of his tribe, for the Indians were admitted among the ranks of the Americans, upon condition that they would abstain from their horrible custom of scalping their victims. On the evening of the battle of . . ., C. came and sat himself down by the fire of our bivouac. I asked him what had been his fortune that day: he related his exploits; and growing warm and animated by the recollection of them, he concluded by suddenly opening the breast of his coat, saying, ‘You must not betray me—see here!’ And I actually beheld,” said the Major, “between his body and his shirt, the skin and hair of an English head, still dripping with gore.”]

The Black American, who earnestly wishes to mingle his race with the European, cannot do so, while the Native American, who might succeed to a certain extent, disdains even to try. The servility of the one dooms him to slavery; the pride of the other dooms him to death.

I remember that while I was traveling through the forests that still cover the State of Alabama, I came one day to the log house of a pioneer. I did not want to go into the American’s home, so I withdrew to rest for a while by a spring not far off in the woods. While I was there (it was near the Creek territory), a Native American woman appeared, followed by a Black woman and holding by the hand a little white girl of five or six, whom I took to be the pioneer’s daughter. A kind of barbarous luxury adorned the Native American woman’s dress: metal rings hung from her nostrils and ears; her hair, decorated with glass beads, fell loose on her shoulders; and I saw that she was not married, for she still wore the necklace of shells that a bride always lays on the marriage bed. The Black woman was dressed in shabby European clothes. All three came and sat down on the bank of the spring. The young Native American woman took the child in her arms and gave her the fond caresses a mother gives, while the Black woman tried by various small tricks to attract the attention of the young Creole.

In her slightest gestures the child showed a consciousness of superiority that contrasted strangely with her childish weakness, as if she received the attentions of her companions with a kind of condescension. The Black woman sat on the ground before her mistress, watching her smallest wishes, and seemingly torn between strong affection for the child and servile fear. The savage, in the midst of her tenderness, showed an air of freedom and pride that was almost ferocious. I had approached the group and was watching them in silence, but my curiosity probably displeased the Native American woman, for she suddenly rose, pushed the child roughly away from her, and, giving me an angry look, plunged into the thicket. I had often happened to see people of the three races that populate North America gathered in the same place. I had noticed in many different ways the preponderance of the whites. But in the scene I have just described there was something especially touching. A bond of affection united the oppressors with the oppressed here, and nature’s effort to bring them together made the immense distance that prejudice and law had placed between them all the more striking.
The Present and Probable Future Condition of the Native American Tribes Which Inhabit the Territory Possessed by the Union

Gradual disappearance of the native tribes — How it takes place — The miseries that accompany the forced migrations of the Native Americans — The savages of North America had only two ways of escaping destruction: war or civilization — They are no longer able to make war — Why they refused to become civilized when it was in their power, and why they cannot become so now that they want to — The example of the Creeks and Cherokees — The policy of the individual States toward these tribes — The policy of the Federal government.

None of the Native American tribes that once lived in the territory of New England — the Naragansetts, the Mohicans, the Pecots — exists any longer except in human memory. The Lenapes, who received William Penn on the banks of the Delaware a hundred and fifty years ago, have disappeared; and I myself met the last of the Iroquois, who were begging for alms. The nations I have named once covered the country all the way to the seacoast, but today a traveler must go more than a hundred leagues into the interior of the continent to find a Native American. These wild tribes have not only withdrawn; they have been destroyed. *b And as they give way or perish, an immense and growing people takes their place. There is no recorded instance of such prodigious growth or such rapid destruction, and it is not hard to describe how the destruction takes place.

b [ In the thirteen original States there are only 6,273 Native Americans remaining. (See Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, p. 90.) [The decrease is now far greater, and is verging on extinction. See page 360 of this volume.]]

When the Native Americans were the only inhabitants of the wilds from which they have since been driven out, their wants were few. They made their own weapons, their only drink was the water of the brook, and their clothes were the skins of the animals whose flesh fed them.

The Europeans brought firearms, strong liquor, and iron to the savages of North America. They taught them to exchange manufactured cloth for the rough garments that had satisfied their untutored simplicity before. The Native Americans had acquired new tastes without the skills to satisfy them, so they had to turn to the whites’ workmanship. But in return for these goods the savage had nothing to offer except the rich furs that still abounded in his woods. Hunting therefore became necessary, not only to feed himself but to obtain the only goods he could supply to Europe in barter. *c While the natives’ wants were thus increasing, their resources kept shrinking.

c [ In their Report to Congress on February 4, 1829, p. 23, Messrs. Clarke and Cass put it this way: “The time when the Indians generally could supply themselves with food and clothing, without any of the articles of civilized life, has long since passed away. The more remote tribes, beyond the Mississippi, who live where immense herds of buffalo are yet to be found and who follow those animals in their periodical migrations, could more easily than any others recur to the habits of their ancestors, and live without the white man or any of his manufactures. But the buffalo is constantly receding. The smaller animals, the bear, the deer, the beaver, the otter, the muskrat, etc., principally minister to the comfort and support of the Indians; and these cannot be taken without guns, ammunition, and traps. Among the Northwestern Indians particularly, the labor of supplying a family with food is excessive. Day after day is spent by the hunter without success, and during this interval his family must subsist upon bark or roots, or perish. Want and misery are around them and among them. Many die every winter from actual starvation.”

The Native Americans will not live as Europeans do, and yet they can neither survive without them nor live exactly as their fathers did. A fact that I likewise give on official authority shows this. Some members of a tribe on the banks of Lake Superior had killed a European. The American government forbade all trade with the tribe the guilty men belonged to until they were handed over to justice. The measure had the desired effect.]

As soon as a European settlement is formed near the territory the Native Americans occupy, the game animals take alarm. *d Thousands of savages wandering through the forests with no fixed dwelling did not disturb them. But as soon as they hear the continuous sounds of European labor nearby, they begin to flee and retreat to the West, where their instinct tells them they will find deserts of immeasurable extent. “The buffalo is constantly receding,” say Messrs. Clarke and Cass in their Report of the year 1829; “a few years since they approached the base of the Alleghany; and a few years hence they may even be rare upon the immense plains which extend to the base of the Rocky Mountains.” I have been assured that the approach of the whites is often felt in this way at two hundred leagues’ distance from their frontier. Their influence thus reaches tribes whose names are unknown to them, and who suffer the evils of usurpation long before they know who is responsible for their distress. *e

d [ “Five years ago,” says Volney in his “Tableau des Etats-Unis,” p. 370, “in going from Vincennes to Kaskaskia, a territory which now forms part of the State of Illinois, but which at the time I mention was completely wild (1797), you could not cross a prairie without seeing herds of from four to five hundred buffaloes. There are now none remaining; they swam across the Mississippi to escape from the hunters, and more particularly from the bells of the American cows.”]

e [ You can easily confirm what I am saying here by consulting the tabular statement of the Native American tribes living in the United States and its territories. (Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, pp. 90-105.) It shows that the tribes in the center of America are rapidly decreasing, even though the Europeans are still at a considerable distance from them.]

Bold adventurers soon move into the country the Native Americans have abandoned. When they have advanced about fifteen or twenty leagues beyond the outermost frontier of the whites, they begin building homes for civilized beings in the middle of the wilderness. This is done without difficulty, because the territory of a hunting nation is poorly defined. It is the common property of the tribe and belongs to no one in particular, so no individual interests are involved in protecting any part of it.

A few European families, settled in different places at a considerable distance from one another, soon drive away the wild animals that remain between their homes. The Native Americans, who had lived in a kind of abundance, then find it hard to survive, and harder still to obtain the goods for barter that they need.

Driving away their game deprives them of their means of existence, just as effectively as if our farmers’ fields were struck with barrenness. They are reduced, like starving wolves, to prowl through the abandoned woods looking for prey. Their instinctive love of their country attaches them to the soil that gave them birth, *f even after it has stopped yielding anything but misery and death. In the end they are forced to give in and leave. They follow the tracks of the elk, the buffalo, and the beaver, and these wild animals guide them in choosing their future country. Strictly speaking, then, it is not the Europeans who drive away the native inhabitants of America; it is famine that forces them to withdraw. This is a happy distinction that escaped the casuists of former times, and we owe it to modern discovery!

f [ “The Indians,” say Messrs. Clarke and Cass in their Report to Congress, p. 15, “are attached to their country by the same feelings which bind us to ours; and, besides, there are certain superstitious notions connected with the alienation of what the Great Spirit gave to their ancestors, which operate strongly upon the tribes who have made few or no cessions, but which are gradually weakened as our intercourse with them is extended. ‘We will not sell the spot which contains the bones of our fathers,’ is almost always the first answer to a proposition for a sale.”]

It is impossible to imagine how much suffering these forced emigrations involve. A people already exhausted and reduced undertake them, and the countries the newcomers go to are inhabited by other tribes, who receive them with jealous hostility. Hunger follows behind them, war awaits them ahead, and misery besets them on every side. Hoping to escape such a host of enemies, they separate, and each individual tries to find the means of supporting his existence in solitude and secrecy, living in the vastness of the wilderness like an outcast in civilized society. The social tie, which distress had long since weakened, then dissolves. They have lost their country, and soon their people desert them. Their very families are wiped out; the names they bore in common are forgotten; their language dies; and every trace of their origin disappears. Their nation has ceased to exist, except in the memory of the antiquaries of America and a few scholars of Europe.

I would be sorry if my reader supposed that I am coloring the picture too strongly. I saw with my own eyes several of the cases of misery I have described, and I witnessed sufferings I have no power to portray.

At the end of the year 1831, while I was on the left bank of the Mississippi at a place the Europeans named Memphis, a numerous band of Choctaws arrived (or Chactas, as the French in Louisiana call them). These savages had left their country and were trying to reach the right bank of the Mississippi, where they hoped to find the refuge the American government had promised them. It was the middle of winter, and the cold was unusually severe. The snow had frozen hard on the ground, and the river was carrying huge masses of ice. The Native Americans had their families with them, and they brought in their train the wounded and the sick, newborn children, and old men on the verge of death. They had neither tents nor wagons, only their weapons and some provisions. I watched them embark to cross the mighty river, and that solemn sight will never fade from my memory. No cry, no sob was heard among the assembled crowd; all were silent. Their calamities were of long standing, and they knew them to be beyond remedy. The Native Americans had all stepped into the boat that was to carry them across, but their dogs remained on the bank. As soon as these animals saw that their masters were leaving the shore for good, they set up a dismal howl and, plunging all together into the icy waters of the Mississippi, swam after the boat.

The ejection of the Native Americans very often takes place today in a regular and, so to speak, legal manner. When the European population begins to approach the edge of the wilderness inhabited by a savage tribe, the government of the United States usually sends envoys to them. The envoys gather the Native Americans on a large plain, eat and drink with them first, and then address them in the following way: “What have you to do in the land of your fathers? Before long, you must dig up their bones in order to live. In what respect is the country you inhabit better than another? Are there no woods, marshes, or prairies, except where you dwell? And can you live nowhere but under your own sun? Beyond those mountains which you see at the horizon, beyond the lake which bounds your territory on the west, there lie vast countries where beasts of chase are found in great abundance; sell your lands to us, and go to live happily in those solitudes.” After saying this, they lay out before the eyes of the Native Americans firearms, woolen garments, kegs of brandy, glass necklaces, tinsel bracelets, earrings, and mirrors. *g If, after seeing all these riches, the Native Americans still hesitate, it is hinted that they have no means of refusing the consent that is demanded, and that the government itself will soon be unable to protect their rights. What are they to do? Half convinced and half forced, they go to live in new deserts, where the importunate whites will not let them stay in peace for ten years. This is how the Americans obtain, at a very low price, whole provinces that the richest sovereigns of Europe could not buy. *h

g [ See, in the Legislative Documents of Congress (Doc. 117), the account of what happens on these occasions. This curious passage comes from the report mentioned above, made to Congress by Messrs. Clarke and Cass in February, 1829. Mr. Cass is now the Secretary of War.

“The Indians,” says the report, “reach the treaty-ground poor and almost naked. Large quantities of goods are taken there by the traders, and are seen and examined by the Indians. The women and children become importunate to have their wants supplied, and their influence is soon exerted to induce a sale. Their improvidence is habitual and unconquerable. The gratification of his immediate wants and desires is the ruling passion of an Indian. The expectation of future advantages seldom produces much effect. The experience of the past is lost, and the prospects of the future disregarded. It would be utterly hopeless to demand a cession of land, unless the means were at hand of gratifying their immediate wants; and when their condition and circumstances are fairly considered, it ought not to surprise us that they are so anxious to relieve themselves.”]

h [ On May 19, 1830, Mr. Edward Everett stated before the House of Representatives that the Americans had already acquired by treaty, to the east and west of the Mississippi, 230,000,000 acres. In 1808 the Osages gave up 48,000,000 acres for an annual payment of $1,000. In 1818 the Quapaws gave up 29,000,000 acres for $4,000. They kept for themselves a territory of 1,000,000 acres as a hunting ground. A solemn oath was taken that it would be respected, but before long it was invaded like the rest. Mr. Bell, in his Report of the Committee on Indian Affairs, February 24, 1830, has these words: “To pay an Indian tribe what their ancient hunting-grounds are worth to them, after the game is fled or destroyed, as a mode of appropriating wild lands claimed by Indians, has been found more convenient, and certainly it is more agreeable to the forms of justice, as well as more merciful, than to assert the possession of them by the sword. Thus the practice of buying Indian titles is but the substitute which humanity and expediency have imposed, in place of the sword, in arriving at the actual enjoyment of property claimed by the right of discovery, and sanctioned by the natural superiority allowed to the claims of civilized communities over those of savage tribes. Up to the present time so invariable has been the operation of certain causes, first in diminishing the value of forest lands to the Indians, and secondly in disposing them to sell readily, that the plan of buying their right of occupancy has never threatened to retard, in any perceptible degree, the prosperity of any of the States.” (Legislative Documents, 21st Congress, No. 227, p. 6.)]

These are great evils, and I must add that they seem to me beyond remedy. I believe that the native nations of North America are doomed to perish, and that once the Europeans are established on the shores of the Pacific Ocean, that race of men will be no more. *i The Native Americans had only two alternatives, war or civilization. In other words, they had to either destroy the Europeans or become their equals.

i [ Almost all American statesmen seem, in fact, to hold this opinion. “Judging of the future by the past,” says Mr. Cass, “we cannot err in anticipating a progressive diminution of their numbers, and their eventual extinction, unless our border should become stationary, and they be removed beyond it, or unless some radical change should take place in the principles of our intercourse with them, which it is easier to hope for than to expect.”]

When the colonies were first settled, the Native Americans might have been able, by uniting their forces, to rid themselves of the small bodies of strangers landing on their continent. *j They tried several times and were on the point of succeeding. But today the disproportion between their resources and those of the whites is too great for such an undertaking to be considered. Nevertheless, from time to time men of penetration do arise among them who foresee the final destiny awaiting the native population and who strive to unite all the tribes in common hostility to the Europeans. Their efforts are in vain. The tribes near the whites are too weakened to offer effective resistance. The others give way to the childish carelessness about tomorrow that marks savage life, and wait until danger is close before preparing to meet it. Some are unable to make the effort, the others unwilling.

j [ Among other warlike enterprises was one by the Wampanaogs and other confederate tribes under Metacom in 1675 against the colonists of New England; the English were also engaged in war in Virginia in 1622.]
It is easy to foresee that the Native Americans will never adapt to civilization, or that it will be too late whenever they may be inclined to try.

Civilization is the result of a long social process that takes place in one spot and is handed down from one generation to the next, each profiting from the experience of the one before. Of all nations, those that live habitually by hunting submit to civilization with the most difficulty. Pastoral tribes, it is true, often change their place of abode, but they follow a regular order in their migrations and often return to their old stations, whereas the hunter’s dwelling changes with that of the animals he pursues.

Several attempts have been made to spread knowledge among the Native Americans without controlling their wandering tendencies, by the Jesuits in Canada and by the Puritans in New England. *k None of these efforts was crowned with any lasting success. Civilization began in the cabin, but it soon withdrew to die in the woods. The great error of these lawgivers to the Native Americans was that they did not understand that, to civilize a people, one must first make it settle, and this cannot be done without inducing it to cultivate the soil. The Native Americans should first have been accustomed to agriculture. But not only do they lack this indispensable first step toward civilization, they would have great difficulty acquiring it. Men who have once given themselves up to the restless and adventurous life of the hunter feel an insurmountable disgust for the constant and regular labor that farming requires. We see this proved within our own society, but it is far more visible among peoples whose fondness for the chase is part of their national character.
k [ See the “Histoire de la Nouvelle France,” by Charlevoix, and the work entitled “Lettres edifiantes.”]

Apart from this general difficulty, there is another that applies especially to the Native Americans: they consider labor not merely an evil but a disgrace, so that their pride keeps them from becoming civilized as much as their indolence does. *l

l [ “In all the tribes,” says Volney, in his “Tableau des Etats-Unis,” p. 423, “there still exists a generation of old warriors, who cannot forbear, when they see their countrymen using the hoe, from exclaiming against the degradation of ancient manners, and asserting that the savages owe their decline to these innovations; adding, that they have only to return to their primitive habits in order to recover their power and their glory.”]

There is no Native American so wretched that he does not keep, under his hut of bark, a lofty idea of his personal worth. He considers the cares of industry and labor degrading occupations. He compares the farmer to the ox that draws the furrow, and even in our most ingenious handicrafts he sees nothing but the work of slaves. It is not that he lacks admiration for the power and intellectual greatness of the whites. But although the results of our efforts amaze him, he despises the means by which we achieve them, and while he acknowledges our ascendancy, he still believes in his own superiority. War and hunting are the only pursuits that seem to him worthy of a man. *m In the dreary solitude of his woods, the Native American cherishes the same ideas and opinions as the noble of the Middle Ages in his castle, and to complete the resemblance he needs only to become a conqueror. Thus, strange as it may seem, it is in the forests of the New World, and not among the Europeans who populate its coasts, that the ancient prejudices of Europe still survive.

m [ The following description appears in an official document: “Until a young man has been engaged with an enemy, and has performed some acts of valor, he gains no consideration, but is regarded nearly as a woman. In their great war-dances all the warriors in succession strike the post, as it is called, and recount their exploits. On these occasions their auditory consists of the kinsmen, friends, and comrades of the narrator. The profound impression which his discourse produces on them is manifested by the silent attention it receives, and by the loud shouts which hail its termination. The young man who finds himself at such a meeting without anything to recount is very unhappy; and instances have sometimes occurred of young warriors, whose passions had been thus inflamed, quitting the war-dance suddenly, and going off alone to seek for trophies which they might exhibit, and adventures which they might be allowed to relate.”]

More than once in the course of this work I have tried to explain the prodigious influence that social condition seems to have on the laws and customs of men, and I ask leave to add a few words on the same subject.

When I perceive the resemblance between the political institutions of our ancestors the Germans and those of the wandering tribes of North America, and between the customs described by Tacitus and those I have sometimes witnessed, I cannot help thinking that the same cause has produced the same results in both hemispheres. I think that amid the apparent diversity of human affairs, a certain number of primary facts can be discovered from which all the others derive. In what we usually call the German institutions, then, I am inclined to see only barbarian habits, and in what we call feudal principles, the opinions of savages.
